points.t: Dry, cracked **‘crazy-paving’ shins** or generalised itch, worse in winter after hot baths and soaps.
Age-related **barrier lipid loss** + environment, drugs, comorbidities → xerosis → fissures → itch–scratch.
Liberal **greasy emollients** and soap substitutes daily; short **moderately potent** steroid for flares.
Itch out of proportion to rash: **scabies**, **bullous pemphigoid**, systemic disease (CKD, cholestasis, lymphoma).

cause.lead: Older skin holds less water and repairs slowly.
points: **Ageing epidermis**: fewer lipids and NMF, slower repair, more water loss, less sebum and sweat.
**Environment**: low humidity, central heating, hot showers, soaps, antiseptic washes.
**Drugs**: diuretics, **statins**, retinoids, some antiandrogens, chemotherapy / EGFR inhibitors.
**Systemic**: hypothyroidism, CKD, diabetes, malnutrition, HIV, malignancy (acquired ichthyosis).

visuals.caption: When barrier lipids are lost, water escapes and irritants get in: the same ‘bricks and mortar’ failure drives dry, itchy older skin.

features.lead: From dry skin to eczema craquelé, and the patterns around it.
points: Dull rough scale, tight feel, **nocturnal itch**, winter flares.
**Asteatotic eczema**: shallow red fissures in a cracked-porcelain network on shins.
**Venous eczema**: medial gaiter area, haemosiderin, oedema, varicose veins.
**Discoid**: coin-shaped weeping plaques. **Lichen simplex / prurigo**: thick scratched plaques or nodules.
Skin of colour: redness may look violaceous or grey-brown; judge scale and thickening.

visuals.caption: Asteatotic eczema (eczema craquelé): a network of shallow red fissures between dry polygonal plates on both shins.

items.name: Nodular prurigo
items.t: Excoriated firm nodules at reachable sites.

points: Season, bathing, products, drugs, care-home contacts.
New generalised itch or resistant: systemic screen and don’t-miss list.
Swab only if infected; patch test if products seem to worsen it.

cards.name: Scabies
cards.clue: Burrows, night itch, itchy contacts or care home.

cards.name: Pre-bullous pemphigoid
cards.clue: Urticated plaques, intense itch, older adult: refer.

cards.name: Systemic itch
cards.clue: Little rash; weight loss, night sweats, nodes.

manage.lead: Emollient prevents the next flare; steroid treats this one.

points: Emollients **liberally and often** (≥ 2–3 times daily, after washing); greasier on legs; urea 5–10% for scale.
Soap substitutes; short lukewarm showers; pat dry; humidify; cotton clothes.
Asteatotic flare: short **moderately potent** steroid (e.g. clobetasone butyrate) 1–2 weeks + emollient.
Thick leg plaques: potent, short term.
Venous eczema: emollient + steroid + compression after ABPI.
Lichen simplex / prurigo: potent steroid ± occlusion; refer if refractory.
Infected: per NICE; avoid routine topical antibiotics.
Review diuretics / statins **with the GP**: don’t stop cardiovascular drugs unilaterally.

visuals.caption: Help older people reach their legs: a long-handled applicator, a pump dispenser, and a non-slip mat because emollients make floors slippery.
visuals.alt: Older woman applying emollient with a long-handled applicator

limits.t: Emollients on fabrics: no smoking or naked flames; wash clothing often (MHRA).
Slippery floors: non-slip mats; apply after stepping out.

items.t: Intense itch with **urticated plaques**: consider pemphigoid; refer.
Generalised itch with weight loss, night sweats or nodes: systemic work-up.
Suspected **scabies outbreak** in a care home.
Non-healing ‘eczema’: patch test or rethink the diagnosis.

pearls.t: ‘Steroid settles it but it always comes back’ = **no maintenance emollient**.
Teach fingertip units, and involve carers.

quiz.q: Commonest cause of itch in older adults?
Two drug classes that dry the skin?
quiz.a: Diuretics and statins (also retinoids, antiandrogens, EGFR inhibitors).

quiz.q: Itch with urticated plaques in an 80-year-old?

quiz.a: Short moderately potent course (e.g. clobetasone butyrate) 1–2 weeks with ongoing emollient.
